I'm also pretty new and have started painting Mouselings from Reaper miniatures.

First I clean them, they have some extra flashing that needs to be removed. I do that with snips, then sand/file areas that need that. After that I take and old toothbrush and soapy water and scrub them to remove any oils from the production process and handling.

Second, I prime them. I use black. (Just a cheap spray can from the hardware store) Some people swear by grey or white. It depends on what your overall color scheme is. By using black if I don't have perfect coverage it's a built in shadow, but it's harder to achieve brighter colors with thin layers of paint. A trade-off. I sketched mine and used colored pencils to decide on my pallette and wanted a darker scheme, so black works for me.

I paint in the order that they get dressed, so skin/fur first, then any clothing that goes over that then anything that layers on the clothing.

After that I do a ink wash to give better shadows, then drybrush some highlights. At this point I'll really get in to do fine details, like eyeball and pupils.

Adding some terrain to the base of the figure, so sand or stone or grass, really makes everything look better.

Finally, since these are going to be handled an acrylic clear coat will protect your work. They sell matte or gloss depending on what effect you are going for.

  1. Clean
  2. Prime
  3. Base-Colors
  4. Ink Wash
  5. Drybrush
  6. Basing
  7. Clear coat

Purchases: Primer - Spray can of primer

Paints/washes - I already had artists acrylics, so I just use those. I've never used "model" paints, so can't comment on their quality. I will say that painting an army would be more consistent, because you can buy specific colors rather than mixing your own. You can buy washes as well, or

Brushes - Again, I already had some brushes, but I did need to pick up a few small brushes to be able to do the fine detail work. Old brushes work well for dry brushing.

Basing - You can buy flock and sand and grass tufts, or you can find stones outside.

Clear coat - Not too expensive and not required, just my preference to keep things protected.

ETA:

You can probably get a really cheap "learn to paint" thing from Michael's that will have more than enough to get you started. It would come with small brushes and a selection of small tubes of paint. Opt for acrylic rather than oil, because it's easier to clean up brushes and such. You don't HAVE to prime the figures, but it will make the process of painting easier. The basing and clear coating aren't necessary either, but add to the final product.

Get a palette. Watch lots of video tutorials. Dr fausts painting clinic (or something like that) is really good on youtube, but there are many others. Thin your paints. (with water or medium, I think water works just fine) Get some paints, and a few washes. Learn to take care of your brushes (just google it). Then you just have to practice a lot. You might want to find some tutorials on how to strip paint off figures as well, so you can paint figures and get better, and then go back and strip and repaint the one you painted first which you may think turned out shitty.
